sub: Putting drone traffic on the map — literally

title: Geodata for Flight Route Planning
desc: A drone route is a query against many geographic layers at once

body.card: The layers a route planner needs
items: Geo-zones — no-fly and restricted zones (airports, hospitals, prisons, nature reserves)
Terrain & obstacles — elevation models, buildings, power lines, cranes
Population density — ground risk depends on who is below; in the Specific category (Module 1) the SORA risk assessment scores exactly that before a flight is authorised
Weather layers — wind fields and precipitation as time-dependent rasters
Live traffic — other drones and manned aviation, streamed in real time (Modules 12, 6, 8)
Live positions rendered on the map — the FlightAware picture from Module 1, now for unmanned traffic
Track history, planned route and actual route in one view: instant anomaly detection for operators

title: Applications & the German Data Source
desc: Logistics, rescue services — and where the official geo-zones come from

items: Logistics — corridor planning for delivery routes, automatically re-routed around temporary geo-zones
Rescue services — fastest legal route for a medical-supply drone, computed against live airspace data
Inspection & monitoring — pipelines, railways and power lines flown along precise geo-referenced paths
Germany's official digital platform for unmanned aviation (BMDV / DFS)
Interactive map of all geographic zones relevant for drone flights — the authoritative source for German operations
Machine-readable access makes it a natural data layer for every route planner discussed on the previous slide

body.caption: DiPUL map tool: every colored layer is a rule your route planner must respect (Berlin region shown)

title: From Telemetry to a Moving Map
desc: The 'real-time' in real-time GIS — how a live position becomes a moving dot

items: The drone emits a position several times per second; Spring WebFlux (M8) pushes each fix to the browser over SSE or WebSocket — no polling
Each fix travels as a GeoJSON point in WGS84 (lat / lon) — the format every map library speaks
The map redraws only the features that moved, so hundreds of live tracks stay smooth
Base map: raster or vector tiles (OpenStreetMap with MapLibre, Leaflet or OpenLayers) — all open-source
Overlays: DiPUL geo-zones underneath, planned route and the live track on top
Coordinate care: tiles are Web Mercator (EPSG:3857), data is WGS84 (EPSG:4326) — mixing them up is the classic first bug

body.alt: Leaflet map of Sigmaringen with a dashed planned route, solid live track, current drone position marker and a red hospital geo-zone
body.caption: The stack in action (Leaflet + OSM): planned route, live track via SSE, DiPUL-style geo-zone — around our campus in Sigmaringen. Project idea #5 is exactly this slice.

title: The Last Twenty Lines: SSE to Leaflet
desc: What one position fix looks like on the wire — and the browser code that moves the dot

body.code: // one fix, as the Module 8 endpoint streams it (text/event-stream) data: {"type":"Feature", "geometry":{"type":"Point","coordinates":[9.2160, 48.0877]}, "properties":{"droneId":"mini4-01","altMeters":38.5,"ts":"2026-08-26T10:15:02Z"}} // browser — subscribe once, move the marker on every fix const src = new EventSource("/tracks"); // Flux<TrackUpdate> from Module 8 src.onmessage = e => { const fix = JSON.parse(e.data); const [lon, lat] = fix.geometry.coordinates; // GeoJSON: lon, lat — Leaflet: lat, lon marker.setLatLng([lat, lon]); track.addLatLng([lat, lon]); // L.polyline — the solid live track };

items: Coordinate order: GeoJSON is [lon, lat], Leaflet wants [lat, lon] — swap them and the drone flies off the coast of Somalia
EventSource reconnects by itself but replays nothing — gaps after a dropped connection are filled from the topic (Module 9), not by the browser
Ten fixes a second per drone is more than any map can draw — throttle at the source with sample() (Module 8), not in the browser
A drone route is a query across many geographic layers at once — geo-zones, terrain, population density, weather and live traffic
The real-time layer is the hard part: live positions streamed onto a moving map turn Module 1's manned-traffic picture into an unmanned one
Authoritative data matters — in Germany, DiPUL is the official, machine-readable source of drone geo-zones
This closes the loop: telemetry from your DJI drone (5) flows through the backend (7–10) and is rendered on the map here
